Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: Until 1963, this species was only known to occur in Sarawak (Mertens 1963), and it is still thought likely to be endemic to northwestern Borneo. The current species distribution in Borneo largely coincides with tectonic terrains (cf. Yap 2002, Auliya 2006). All records of Lanthanotus to date have been reported on the “East Malaya Terrane” (see Michaux 1995). The absence of records of Lanthanotus in the remainder of Kalimantan, Brunei Darussalam and Sabah, especially in well-surveyed areas of Sabah, and its recent discovery further south in the East Malaya Terrane, supports this assumption. The species is thought to have been lost from most historical localities following forest clearance, with any surviving subpopulations of any significance in Sarawak likely to be restricted to the Niah Caves region and the upper Baleh region, although there have been no records from Niah for the past 30 years (I. Das pers. comm. 2020). Known extant or recently extant subpopulations are known from only five of 13 historical localities, although a number of the others have imprecise locality data (I. Das pers. comm. 2019).
documentation.population:
Between 1877 and 1961 only 12 specimens were found (Proud 1978). In 2004, Eric Pianka noted that “only about 100 of these lizards have ever been collected”, all recorded and collected from Sarawak (Das and Yaakob 2007). One specimen was reported from West Kalimantan in 2008 (Yaap et al. 2012). In 2013, again one specimen was reported from northeastern East Kalimantan (a locality now in North Kalimantan) (Vergner 2013). These are the only records that have been published to date. In 2014, rumours were spread that c. 36 live specimen were circulated in the pet trade in Germany.

In total, therefore, c. 150 individuals have been reported since the discovery of this species 143 years ago (Steindachner 1877). Due to the extremely low numbers of live specimens known to have been collected alive (implying that c. one specimen would have been collected annually in the period 1877–2014), it must be considered that this lizard remains exceptionally rare even though the greater number of recent records circulated through the Internet appear to give the impression that the species may not be that rare. Live specimens have been become available in e.g., Japan, Czech Republic, Russia, France, Germany and the USA, however, no qualitative information is available to assess the species’ current population status and population trends. In 2014, a survey carried out in the northern central part of West Kalimantan recorded 19 live specimens (Langner 2017), and attempts to explain this “relative high density” need to be treated with care, as should the claim that it is possible to conclude that the species can persist in “heavily anthropogenically influenced environments”. The Borneo Earless Monitor has undoubtedly suffered declines and likely local extinctions as a result of forest clearance, as while its ecology is poorly-known it seems to be reliant on forest, and since the earless monitor entered the international pet trade a decrease in numbers at least within local subpopulations must be inferred in addition to the impacts of still-ongoing degradation and fragmentation of natural habitats in all range states. The species remains too poorly-known for rates of decline to be inferred, but a rate of decline in excess of 30% over three generations driven mainly by habitat loss is considered to be plausible despite an absence of information on the species' generation length..
documentation.habitats: The species inhabits lowland localities in northwestern Borneo, and appears in particular to be associated with lowland rainforests in the vicinity of streams. It has also been reported from agricultural lands, but only in the vicinity of forests and it is considered to require primary forests or at least those with good canopy cover and freshwater. Recent observations indicate a preference for undisturbed lowland forests with clear, rocky streams. It is a nocturnal, cryptozoic species, daylight hours being spent in a semi-torpid condition in retreats such as burrows in the soil up to about 30 cm, along riverbanks or under rocks and rotting logs. At night, it forages on land and in water. The species reportedly preys on earthworms (see http://lanthanotus-org.webs.com/), freshwater crabs and catfish (in litt. 12 August 2015 to M. Auliya), and captive specimens also take chopped red meat and live goldfish.  A 44 cm specimen was recorded with six eggs (Proud 1978). Four to six eggs have been reported in a Facebook post accessed in 2016, reporting breeding in a captive animal in Japan. Specimens outside Borneo have reportedly reproduced, observing eggs and hatchlings; some of these, however, may also have derived from gravid females. Gestation period has been reported around 130 days (http://s592754522.website-start.de/artenteil/lanthanotus-borneensis/  - accessed 24 April 2016). The period of incubation has been reported between 70–80 days (http://www.varanus.net/forums/read.php?2,36151,36155#msg-36155 - accessed 24 April 2016, but no longer accessible). Thus, more than six months pass from fertilization to hatching. To date no F2 generation has been reported, thus information on age at maturity is lacking in both sexes. Due to the paucity of reproductive data, no information can be provided on generation length.
documentation.threats:
Deforestation and conversion to agricultural land are known to have a severe impact on species richness of forest herpetofauna (cf. Sodhi et al. 2010). A relative recent study highlighted the increase of destruction of lowland forests on Borneo until 2010; results therein indicate that more than 30% of Borneo’s lowland forests had vanished in the period 1973–2010 due to logging, fires and conversion to plantations (Gaveau et al. 2014). This is expected to have had serious impacts on this lowland forest lizard, and Global Forest Watch data indicate a loss of 24% forest cover in Sarawak, where most known records of this species have been taken, between 2000 and 2018, and it is presumed to have been lost from localities where forest no longer remains. One reported locality in Miri Division is in an area where logging operations recently began (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2014).

There is only limited knowledge of the life history of the Earless Monitor, however, reduced canopy cover, the drainage of small water bodies and changes in riverine microhabitats are likely to have an impact on its long-term survival (also cf. Wanger et al. 2010).

The uniqueness of the species has triggered an enormous herpetocultural interest and demand on an international level. Since traders have spotted potential collecting sites the species has created a market; the species appears to have entered the pet trade immediately after the discovery of a subpopulation in West Kalimantan, and this state is believed to be the origin of most animals in captivity. The Earless Monitor has been recorded in very small numbers over a period of a century and a half, and individual subpopulations are expected to be small. Collecting pressure therefore represents a severe threat to any viable subpopulations that are discovered.
documentation.measures:
There are no conservation actions in place for Lanthanotus. It remains difficult to ascertain the impacts of major threats impacting on the species. It is consequently not possible to assess the impact intentional collecting has compared to the conversion of forest habitats that may threaten the viability of local subpopulations. Despite being nationally totally protected in its range States of Borneo, this measure does not protect the species from being smuggled out of its range States. International trade in this species may be regulated with a listing on CITES. Malaysia has proposed to list the species in CITES Appendix I (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/cop/17/prop/MY_Lanthanotidae.pdf). However, the proposal was rejected and amended for inclusion in Appendix II, “with a zero quota for wild specimens for commercial trade” (https://lanthanotus-org.webs.com/2016-CITES_decisions-on-amendment-proposals-1.pdf). However, this amendment includes the option to launder juvenile wild-captured specimens as captive-bred to international destinations.

Most important conservation measures are to manage (prevent) harvest and trade. It is further a prerequisite to inform and train authorities and relevant stakeholders. Besides, locality records and relevant sites where the species occurs need to be monitored/managed; in protected areas park staff needs to control illegal collecting activities.
documentation.use_trade:
It is assumed that trade in the species was initially reported in 2012, and there are indications (evidence cannot be provided) that live specimens offered for sale have been sourced from West Kalimantan. The first occurrence of the species in Indonesian Borneo was published online in September 2012 (Yaap et al. 2012). Although the authors withheld geographic coordinates for fear that this information would be misused by reptile traders, a few months after this discovery was published requests from Indonesian nationals to co-authors of the study were received for more precise locality details of the species in West Kalimantan (in litt. 3 March 2013 to M. Auliya).

In April 2013, a new reptile zoo in Kawazu, Shizuoka, Japan, "i-Zoo”, displayed information and an image of a Lanthanotus feeding on an earthworm, and apparently a female and male specimen were maintained (in litt. 17–18 April 2013 to M. Auliya). According to an informant, these specimens originated from Sarawak, and this information was retrieved long before the issue was internationalized, which was c. end of February 2013 (in litt. 3 September 2015 to M. Auliya) (also see http://izoo.co.jp/cando/pg129.html).

In early June 2014, a pair of the species was first offered in Hamm (Germany), the world’s largest reptile fair by two Czech nationals and by a German national (in litt. 3 June 2014 to M. Auliya).

In July 2014, the species was displayed in Russia and France (in litt. 8 July 2014 to M. Auliya).

In 2014, during a herpetological conference in Germany, a German national reported the discovery of more than 20 specimens; however, according to rumours during that meeting, 36 live specimens were currently located in Germany (in litt. 9 Oct. 2014, to M. Auliya); at this stage this information could not be verified. Information provided in this presentation was planned to be published, and indeed was published by Langner (2017).

Near Kuala Lumpur, in Malaysia, several specimens were for sale; that are also available in Jakarta (in litt. 29 August 2015 to M. Auliya). 

In August 2015, numerous individuals were spotted in West Kalimantan (Pontianak?) for sale; one specimen was distinctly dark almost black and sold to Germany (in litt. 30 August 2015 to M. Auliya).

In 2015, one adult and one juvenile were offered from Sarawak (in litt. 30 August 2015 to M. Auliya).

December 2015, 10 specimens were seized at Jakarta airport (WCS Wildlife Crimes Unit, January 2016).

In March 2016, a seizure of 17 specimens was reported from Supadio airport, Pontianak, West Kalimantan (Indonesia). [http://regional.kompas.com/read/2016/03/15/17180021/Paket.Bertuliskan.Mie.Ramen.Isinya.Biawak.Tak.Bertelinga – date accessed 20 March 2016].

According to the TRAFFIC Newsletter February 2016, the Earless Monitor has been reported from nine countries outside its range, such as USA, Germany, Japan, United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Czech Republic, France, Ukraine and Russia. 
In Oct./Nov. 2017 a seizure of one specimen at Supadio International Airport, West Kalimantan Province, Indonesia was reported.

Anecdotal information exists that one collecting location must refer to the Landak region in West Kalimantan highlighted by Yaap et al. (2012); should this be the case, the initial precautionary approach to refrain more precise locality data has proven otherwise.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Endangered on the basis that this species is known from only around 150 specimens collected over a century and a half at fewer than 15 confirmed localities, a number of which are likely to have been lost following deforestation, and the surviving population is considered to be severely fragmented. The species' true area of occupancy is unknown, but the known records correspond to an area of occupancy of 52 km<sup>2</sup>. The species' presumed natural absence from much of Borneo and apparent reliance on lowland forest suggest that it could well be below 2,000 km<sup>2</sup>, and a precautionary approach is adopted here to infer that it is below 500 km<sup>2</sup>. Habitat loss driven by various processes is ongoing within its range while a recently-emerged threat from collection for the pet trade is expected to seriously threaten at least some remaining subpopulations. While rates of forest loss within its range have been a little below 30% in 18 years and nothing is known of this species' generation length, its reliance on a specific lowland forest habitat at elevated risk could indicate that rates of decline in suitable habitat - and by inference in this lizard - have exceeded 30% in three generations. Of five subpopulations known or presumed to be extant, one is in an area where logging began two years ago, and at least one appears to have been targeted by traders. Nothing is known about the viability of any extant subpopulation.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Reviewed by McDowell and Bogert (1954), McDowell (1967), Mertens (1961) and Underwood (1957). Based on a study of the structure of the ears, McDowell (1967) considered the family to be closely related to the extinct Mosasauridae from the Cretaceous and Rieppel (1983) showed that the only living species in the family, Lanthanotus borneensis (Steindachner, 1878), exhibits no special similarities with primitive snakes in his study of cranial structure. Rieppel (1980) showed that the genus Lanthanotus Steindachner, 1878, forms the sister-taxon of Varanus, the two lineages together forming the sister-taxon of the New World Heloderma.
